analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover breast, cervical, colon, and prostate cancer screening at set ages.
analysis.headline: Introduced February 2, 2010, the bill was referred to four House committees and their health subcommittees and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required nearly all health insurance — employer plans, individual-market policies, and the plan covering federal employees — to pay for cancer screening: yearly mammograms for women 40 and older, yearly Pap tests and pelvic exams for women 18 and older, colon cancer screening starting at 50, and prostate screening for men 50 and older, with earlier screening for people at high risk. Insurers could not drop someone just to escape the rule and could not pressure doctors to skip required care, and plans would have to send members a printed annual summary of what is covered and what it costs. Plans could still charge deductibles and copays, as long as those charges treated the screenings the same as other benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Insured workers and families, people buying their own coverage, and federal employees: anyone whose plan did not already pay for these screenings would get a guaranteed benefit at the ages or risk levels spelled out in the bill, plus an annual printed summary of covered benefits, cost sharing, and network doctors. People with a family history, a previous cancer, or a known gene marker would qualify for earlier screening, and Black men would qualify for earlier prostate screening.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured adults due for cancer screenings

how_it_helps.text: Group health plans and insurers would have to pay for annual mammograms for women 40 and older (or high-risk younger women), annual clinical breast exams for women 40 and older (every three years for average-risk women 20 to 40), annual Pap tests and pelvic exams for women 18 and older, colorectal cancer screening for adults 50 and older (or high-risk younger adults), and prostate screening for men 50 and older (or high-risk younger men, including Black men and men with a family history).

Plans could not refuse to enroll or renew someone just to dodge the screening requirement, could not pay individuals to accept weaker protections, and could not penalize or reward providers for deviating from it.

Plans and issuers would have to disclose, at enrollment and at least annually in print, what is covered, the deductibles and copays, out-of-pocket maximums, balance-billing exposure, and provider network details.

The same screening guarantee would extend to individual-market coverage and the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and the HHS Secretary could update the required screenings as medical practice evolves — without ever reducing the mandated coverage.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers and workers who fund group plans would bear the added screening claims, recovered through premiums; the federal employees' program would absorb the same cost. Plans could still pass deductibles and copays on to patients.

drawbacks.text: Plans could still impose deductibles, coinsurance, and copays on the required screenings as long as the charges did not discriminate against them, so a "covered" test could still carry real out-of-pocket cost for a patient.

The bill locked in a one-size schedule — annual mammograms from age 40, annual Pap tests from 18, routine prostate testing from 50 — that was more aggressive than the preventive-medicine guidance issued around the same time, which favored less frequent screening for some groups; more screening means more false positives and more unnecessary follow-up procedures.

The mandate would have reached employer plans, individual-market policies, and federal employees' insurance alike, so the added screening claims would be financed through higher premiums and program costs across the board — an honest supporter would acknowledge the benefit is not free.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Early detection is the strongest tool against these four cancers — colorectal screening can prevent cancer outright by removing precancerous growths, and cervical screening catches treatable precancerous cells — so the coverage guarantee had real value, especially for anyone whose plan skimped on screening. Against that: the bill let plans keep charging deductibles and copays, its fixed schedule was stricter than the screening guidance issued around the same time (raising false-positive risk), and the added claims would come back as premiums. As it happened, Congress enacted the Affordable Care Act weeks after this bill was introduced, requiring most new plans to cover recommended preventive services, including many of these screenings, with no patient cost-sharing — so the same ground was largely covered by other means even though this bill died.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in early February 2010, the bill was sent to four House committees and then to three health subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Representative Carolyn Maloney introduced the bill on February 2, 2010 and delivered introductory remarks the same day.
It was referred the same day to four House committees — Energy and Commerce (the primary referral), Education and Labor, Ways and Means, and Oversight and Government Reform.

Within three weeks it was passed down to health subcommittees: Energy and Commerce's Health Subcommittee on February 3, Education and Labor's Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions Subcommittee on February 23, and a Health Subcommittee on February 24.
The record shows no hearing, markup, amendment, floor vote, or further action of any kind for the rest of the 111th Congress, which ended January 3, 2011.
The bill's only recorded support was its sponsor and three Democratic cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers were spared a new screening mandate. Patients lost little in practice: the Affordable Care Act, enacted weeks after this bill was introduced, required most new plans to cover recommended preventive services — including many of these same cancer screenings — with no patient cost-sharing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers avoided the mandate

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held. The only recorded support was Democratic — one sponsor and three cosponsors out of 253 House Democrats — and no member of either party is recorded as taking any action for or against the bill.

industries.note: The bill would force coverage and payment for a defined slate of cancer screenings across employer plans, the individual market, and federal employees' insurance, with costs recovered through premiums. Its interest lay in keeping that obligation off its books; the mandate existed to close coverage gaps for patients.

industries.industry: Employers and plan sponsors (self-funded ERISA plans)
industries.note: Self-funded employer plans would carry the same screening mandate, with the cost landing in total compensation and premiums; workers would get the guaranteed benefit in return.

industries.industry: Screening providers and laboratories (mammography facilities, cytology labs, gastroenterologists)
industries.note: Guaranteed screening volume for certified mammography facilities, pathology labs, and screening physicians, paid at plan rates; more early detections also shift care toward more treatable stages.
